learningObjective: Shared glucose monitoring requires an appropriate device and validated processing.

title: Glucose round workflow
stem: A nurse checks several clients' glucose levels. Which practices reduce cross-contamination? Select all that apply.
options: Change gloves and clean hands between clients
Store used lancets beside clean test strips
Process the shared meter after each use as instructed
Keep clean supplies separated from used equipment

Used sharps should be immediately contained, not mixed with supplies.
Manufacturer-directed processing reduces device-mediated transmission.
Separation protects supplies that will contact other clients.
takeaway: Organize glucose testing to separate clean supplies from blood exposure.
learningObjective: Organize glucose testing to separate clean supplies from blood exposure.

title: Contaminated medication cart
stem: After checking a client's bleeding wound, a nurse touches the shared medication-cart handle with used gloves. What is the best correction?

Change gloves only before the next wound dressing
Wipe the gloves and continue the round
Cover the handle with paper for the remainder of the shift

Wiping used gloves does not reliably restore their cleanliness.
Covering contamination does not establish effective disinfection.

learningObjective: Address both contaminated hands and surfaces after a workflow breach.

title: Shared vial at bedside
stem: A multidose vial intended for several clients has been brought into one client's immediate treatment area. What should guide its further use?
options: Return it to clean central stock after wiping the label
Follow injection-safety policy for patient-dedicated use or disposal
Use it for any client with the same diagnosis
Keep it shared if the stopper was not visibly touched
why: Patient-area exposure may make return to shared use inappropriate.
Safe handling considers where shared supplies have been exposed.
Diagnosis matching does not prevent organism transfer.
Absence of visible touch does not establish uncontaminated handling.
takeaway: Protect shared injectable supplies from patient-treatment-area contamination.
learningObjective: Protect shared injectable supplies from patient-treatment-area contamination.

title: Leftovers left overnight
stem: An older adult plans to eat cooked chicken left on the counter overnight because it smells normal. What should the nurse advise?
options: Reheat until it smells freshly cooked
Taste a small portion before deciding
Discard food held unsafely; smell cannot establish safety
Refrigerate it now and eat it tomorrow

takeaway: Do not judge food safety by smell after unsafe storage.
learningObjective: Do not judge food safety by smell after unsafe storage.

title: Raw and ready-to-eat food
stem: During a home visit, raw poultry juice is dripping onto washed salad in the refrigerator. What needs correction?
options: Only the refrigerator door position
Only the salad's serving temperature
Only the date on the poultry package
Discard contaminated ready-to-eat food and separate raw-food storage safely

learningObjective: Keep raw animal-food juices away from ready-to-eat foods.

title: Food-safety teaching
stem: Which practices reduce infection risk when an older adult prepares meals? Select all that apply.
options: Use separate clean preparation surfaces for raw and ready-to-eat food
Taste leftovers to determine whether storage was safe
Refrigerate perishable leftovers promptly in suitable containers
Clean hands and food-contact surfaces during preparation
why: Separation limits transfer of raw-food organisms.
Taste cannot reliably identify dangerous contamination.
Prompt cooling limits microbial growth.
Hand and surface hygiene reduce introduction and spread of organisms.
takeaway: Control food contamination and storage conditions together.
learningObjective: Control food contamination and storage conditions together.

title: Dietary allergen mismatch
stem: A client with a documented severe milk allergy receives a meal tray labelled lactose-free. What should the nurse do?
options: Accept it because lactose-free means milk-free
Verify milk-protein content and obtain an appropriate tray before serving
Ask the client to try a small bite under observation
Remove only visible cheese and serve the remainder

A test bite can provoke an avoidable reaction.
Removing visible components does not reliably remove the allergen.
takeaway: Verify the actual allergen rather than relying on a related dietary label.
learningObjective: Verify the actual allergen rather than relying on a related dietary label.

title: Damp central-line dressing
stem: A client has a central-line dressing saturated after sweating; the next scheduled change is tomorrow. The nurse is competent and authorized for dressing care. What next?
options: Wait until tomorrow to avoid extra manipulation
Tape the wet edges down
Replace the compromised dressing using the approved aseptic procedure
Place a dry towel over it until rounds

Securing wet material does not restore the barrier.

A towel does not re-establish a sterile site covering.

learningObjective: Replace compromised vascular-access dressings rather than waiting for routine timing.

title: Dressing choice for an oozing site
stem: A newly inserted vascular catheter site is oozing small amounts of blood. The authorized, competent nurse follows the device protocol. Which covering is most appropriate while oozing continues?
options: A transparent film without absorbent material despite accumulating fluid
The previous damp dressing reinforced with an outer tape border
A nonsterile absorbent pad placed directly against the insertion site
An appropriate sterile gauze dressing with reassessment of the site
why: Accumulating blood beneath a nonabsorbent film can compromise the site covering.
Reinforcement does not restore a wet compromised barrier.
An invasive insertion site requires an appropriate sterile covering.
Sterile gauze can absorb oozing while protecting the site and permitting planned reassessment.
takeaway: Select the catheter dressing for the actual site condition.
learningObjective: Select the catheter dressing for the actual site condition.

title: Access-port preparation
stem: Before accessing a vascular line, the nurse disinfects the connector but reaches for the syringe while the surface is still wet. What is appropriate?
options: Follow the antiseptic contact/drying instructions before access
Blow on the connector to speed drying
Touch the connector to test whether it is dry
Attach immediately because wetness proves disinfectant is present
why: Required application and drying support effective aseptic access.
Blowing may introduce contamination.
Touching can recontaminate the prepared surface.
Wet presence alone does not establish completion of the labelled process.
takeaway: Complete connector antisepsis according to product and device instructions.
learningObjective: Complete connector antisepsis according to product and device instructions.

title: Vascular-device prevention
stem: A peripheral catheter remains after intravenous treatment has ended. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Review whether the device still has a clinical indication
Retain it indefinitely because replacement might be inconvenient
Assess the site and remove when authorized and no longer required
Document the resulting device plan
why: Device necessity should be reassessed as treatment changes.
Convenience alone does not justify continuing invasive exposure.
Unnecessary catheter time adds avoidable risk.
A clear plan prevents uncertainty across shifts.
takeaway: Remove invasive devices when their indication has ended and removal is authorized.
learningObjective: Remove invasive devices when their indication has ended and removal is authorized.

title: Line protection during bathing
stem: A client with a vascular catheter wants to shower. What should the nurse verify?
options: That water exposure cannot affect a closed infusion
An approved protective method for the site and connections
That the dressing can be changed only after becoming soaked
That tap water is warm enough to disinfect the site

The bathing plan should protect the insertion site and connecting components.

takeaway: Protect catheter sites and connections from water exposure.
learningObjective: Protect catheter sites and connections from water exposure.

title: Two wound-care tasks
stem: The same client has a clean surgical incision and a heavily contaminated draining wound. What should the nurse plan?

Use the same cleansing solution container for both wounds
why: Organisms can transfer between different sites on one client.

Separation and a clean-to-dirty sequence protect the cleaner site.
Shared containers may transfer contamination between wounds.
takeaway: Prevent transfer from contaminated wounds to cleaner sites.
learningObjective: Prevent transfer from contaminated wounds to cleaner sites.

title: Terminal cleaning coordination
stem: A client with infectious diarrhoea transfers out. Another client is waiting for the bed. What should the nurse verify before placement?
options: That fresh linen alone has been applied
That the room no longer has an odour
That the outgoing client took all belongings
That required terminal cleaning and equipment processing are complete
why: Linen change does not disinfect contaminated surfaces.
Odour is not a reliable indicator of contamination.
Belongings removal does not establish environmental processing.
Room readiness depends on the required decontamination process.
takeaway: Confirm environmental readiness before assigning the next client.
learningObjective: Confirm environmental readiness before assigning the next client.

title: Spore-targeted cleaning
stem: A room used by a client with C. difficile is to be disinfected. What should guide product choice?

Any disinfectant that dries most quickly

learningObjective: Match environmental disinfectant activity to the organism and task.

title: Disinfection verification
stem: After an audit finds variable cleaning technique, which observations are useful? Select all that apply.

Whether staff follow device and product compatibility instructions
why: Soil can interfere with subsequent disinfection.

Fragrance does not demonstrate microbial effectiveness.

takeaway: Audit the disinfection process using its actual technical requirements.
learningObjective: Audit the disinfection process using its actual technical requirements.

title: Shared touchscreen contact
stem: Staff use a mobile touchscreen between rooms during direct care. What is an appropriate infection-control plan?
options: Clean it only when fingerprints are visible

why: Visible marks do not identify all contamination.

takeaway: Include shared digital equipment in routine infection-control planning.
learningObjective: Include shared digital equipment in routine infection-control planning.

title: Transport stretcher turnover
stem: A stretcher returns after carrying a client with draining wounds. Which action is needed before the next client?

learningObjective: Process transport equipment between clients according to exposure.

title: Coughing visitor in oncology
stem: A visitor with new cough and fever wants to sit beside an immunocompromised client. What is best?

learningObjective: Adapt visits when symptoms create risk for a vulnerable client.

title: Airborne-room alarm
stem: An airborne-isolation room's pressure alarm signals loss of the intended airflow while an infectious client remains inside. What next?

Move the client to a standard single room as the permanent solution

title: Isolation response readiness

title: Infection precautions and mobility
